While keeping both Eddymurk Crab and Sunderflock is appealing, the extra card advantage from discarding just one creature is significant, and the lands would help cast the expensive Sunderflock.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose to discard Multiversal Passage (and presumably Steam Vents) as 2 non-creature discards
annotations.betterLine: Discard Eddymurk Crab as the sole creature discard, keeping an extra card in hand including the lands needed to eventually cast Sunderflock. With only 1 instant/sorcery in graveyard, Eddymurk Crab would still cost 5+ mana and is the less impactful of the two threats.

annotations.description: Discarded two lands (Multiversal Passage and Steam Vents) instead of discarding a single creature card (Sunderflock). With only 3 lands on board and now 0 lands in hand, they risk missing crucial land drops needed to cast Eddymurk Crab (which costs 5 with current graveyard discount). Sunderflock requires an Elemental already in play to be reasonably castable and is largely a dead card without Eddymurk Crab on board first.
annotations.actionTaken: Discarded Multiversal Passage and Steam Vents (two lands), keeping both Sunderflock and Eddymurk Crab
annotations.betterLine: Discard Sunderflock as the single creature discard, keeping both lands in hand to guarantee land drops on turns 4 and 5, enabling a turn 5 Eddymurk Crab cast

annotations.description: Missed a critical land drop on turn 3 with only 2 lands in play and 8 cards in hand including three playable lands. With Floodfarm Verge, they could have had 3 lands (including WU sources) to hold up No More Lies against the opponent's next turn. Missing this land drop severely delays Day of Judgment (needs 4 mana) and leaves them unable to interact with the opponent's plays.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed priority without playing a land, apparently intending to 'await the moment to strike.'
annotations.betterLine: Play Floodfarm Verge (which enters untapped producing W and U thanks to Hallowed Fountain being a Plains/Island), enabling No More Lies to be held up on the opponent's turn 3, and advancing toward casting Day of Judgment on turn 4.

annotations.description: Casting Consult the Star Charts before playing a land drop is a sequencing error. With only 2 lands in play, Consult looks at 2 cards. If they played a land first (Floodfarm Verge, Sunbillow Verge, or Meticulous Archive), they'd have 3 lands and look at 3 cards instead, giving a strictly better selection. Additionally, casting this spell taps out their mana on turn 3 when the opponent has cards in graveyard that could enable cheap threats, and they have No More Lies in hand that they can no longer hold up.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Consult the Star Charts with only 2 lands in play, looking at 2 cards and tapping out.
annotations.betterLine: Play a land first (Floodfarm Verge or Meticulous Archive) to have 3 lands, making Consult the Star Charts look at 3 cards instead of 2. Alternatively, play the land and hold up No More Lies instead of casting Consult this turn.

annotations.description: Playing Steam Vents as the land drop is suboptimal because they paid 2 life to have it enter untapped (they're at 18 life, suggesting prior shockland payments). With 3 lands already on board and 4 mana available after this land drop, the key consideration is what they need this turn. They have Sleight of Hand and Opt as cantrips, plus counterspells (Spider-Sense, Spell Snare, No More Lies pattern cards). However, the real issue is that Steam Vents provides red mana which isn't needed - their deck appears to be UW with a splash. They already have a Steam Vents on the battlefield. Playing Steam Vents tapped (saving 2 life) would have been fine since they likely just want to hold up counterspell mana (they have 3 untapped lands already). Actually, looking more carefully - they have 3 lands and are playing a 4th. They could cast Sleight of Hand with existing mana before playing the land to see if they find a better land to play. Casting Sleight of Hand first (using 1 of 3 available mana) would let them see 2 cards and potentially find a different/better land, while still being able to play Steam Vents afterward if nothing better shows up.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Steam Vents before casting Sleight of Hand
annotations.betterLine: Cast Sleight of Hand first with existing mana to potentially find a better 4th land drop (like a dual land they actually need), then play whatever land is best. This costs nothing since they have mana available already.

annotations.description: Casting Sleight of Hand (a sorcery) during main phase when holding Opt (an instant) is a sequencing error. With the opponent having 3 mana up (including white and blue for No More Lies or other interaction), casting the sorcery-speed spell taps mana during the main phase unnecessarily. Opt should be preferred here because: 1) Opt can be cast at end of opponent's turn, preserving mana for Spell Snare or Spider-Sense during the opponent's turn. 2) Even if you want to cast a cantrip now, Sleight of Hand adds to graveyard instant/sorcery count for Eddymurk Crab cost reduction either way, but keeping instant-speed options open is better. 3) Casting Sleight now uses one of the 4 mana, leaving only 3 up, when keeping all 4 up would allow both Spell Snare and Spider-Sense as responses. The player could cast Opt at end of opponent's turn instead and keep more mana open this turn.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Sleight of Hand (sorcery) during main phase, using mana proactively
annotations.betterLine: Pass the turn holding up Spell Snare (U) and Spider-Sense (1U) with 4 mana, then cast Opt at end of opponent's turn if nothing needed countering. This preserves maximum flexibility against the opponent's plays while still getting the card selection.

annotations.description: With 4 instants/sorceries in the graveyard (Sleight of Hand x2, Winternight Stories, plus the current Sleight resolving), Eddymurk Crab already costs around 3-4 mana. The player has Steam Vents x2 + Island x2 (4 lands) and already holds Eddymurk Crab. Burst Lightning is a versatile removal/burn spell that would be immediately castable and helps deal with early threats from the opponent's white-blue deck, while also adding to the graveyard count for Eddymurk Crab. Glacial Dragonhunt is a 2-mana sorcery that requires discarding to get the damage effect. While Dragonhunt does have value as card filtering and potential removal, Burst Lightning is more efficient instant-speed removal that can be cast alongside other spells. However, Glacial Dragonhunt does have the harmonize ability for graveyard recursion and the discard synergy with Winternight Stories already in the graveyard. This is close but Burst Lightning's flexibility as instant-speed removal seems slightly better given the opponent could deploy threats.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose Glacial Dragonhunt over Burst Lightning from Sleight of Hand
annotations.betterLine: Take Burst Lightning - it's efficient instant-speed removal that can deal with early threats and serves as a finisher, while Glacial Dragonhunt requires 2 mana at sorcery speed and a discard to get the removal effect

annotations.description: Casting Glacial Dragonhunt as a sorcery with no opposing creatures wastes the damage mode entirely (the 3 damage to a creature has no valid target). Additionally, it taps down to only 1 blue mana, leaving only Spell Snare as protection while the opponent could cast something that Spider-Sense (1U) could counter. Opt would provide card selection while keeping both Spell Snare AND Spider-Sense available.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Glacial Dragonhunt for U/R, using 2 of 3 available mana, with no enemy creatures to target for the damage mode.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Opt for U instead, keeping U+U/R open for both Spell Snare and Spider-Sense as reactive options. Glacial Dragonhunt could be saved for when the opponent has creatures to target with the damage mode.

annotations.description: Glacial Dragonhunt is a 2-mana sorcery on the stack. Kimi25 has No More Lies (W/U) available with exactly the mana to cast it (Hallowed Fountain, Plains, Floodfarm Verge provide W and U). Letting Glacial Dragonhunt resolve allows the opponent to draw a card and potentially deal 3 damage to a creature (though Kimi25 has no creatures, the card draw alone is significant). More importantly, each instant/sorcery in the opponent's graveyard reduces the cost of Eddymurk Crab. The opponent already has 5 cards in their graveyard including instants and sorceries. Letting this resolve adds another spell to the graveyard, making future Eddymurk Crabs cheaper. No More Lies would counter it and exile it (preventing graveyard synergies), and the opponent would need to pay 3 mana they likely don't have available. While countering a card-draw spell with a counterspell is a reasonable use of resources, the decision to let it resolve gives the opponent card advantage and fuels their graveyard strategy for free.
annotations.actionTaken: Declined to counter Glacial Dragonhunt, letting the opponent draw a card and grow their graveyard.
annotations.betterLine: Cast No More Lies targeting Glacial Dragonhunt. The opponent has only 1 untapped land (Steam Vents) and cannot pay the additional {3}. This would exile the spell (denying graveyard synergies for Eddymurk Crab cost reduction and Winternight Stories harmonize), prevent card draw, and is an efficient use of the counterspell against a card-advantage spell.

annotations.description: Seam Rip can target any nonland permanent an opponent controls with mana value 2 or less, not just creatures. However, looking at Sonnet Vorthos's battlefield, they only have lands (Islands and Steam Vents), so there are actually no valid nonland permanent targets. Get Lost also has no valid targets since the opponent has no creatures, enchantments, or planeswalkers. The reasoning about 'no targets' is actually correct for the current board state. However, the player should have played Meticulous Archive from hand as their land drop this turn to advance to 5 lands, enabling future plays like Day of Judgment or kicked Consult the Star Charts. The player had Meticulous Archive in hand and passing without playing a land is a missed land drop.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed priority without playing Meticulous Archive as a land drop first.
annotations.betterLine: Play Meticulous Archive as the land for turn (getting a surveil trigger), then pass. Getting to 5 lands is important for future turns, enabling kicked Consult the Star Charts or leaving up Day of Judgment mana with interaction.

annotations.description: Kimi25 has Seam Rip available for W, which can exile a nonland permanent with mana value 2 or less from the opponent. While the opponent currently has no nonland permanents on the battlefield, Kimi25 also has Meticulous Archive (a tapped land) in hand and could have played it this turn to develop their mana. More importantly, they have 2 untapped lands (Plains and Sunbillow Verge) and chose to pass without playing their land drop (Meticulous Archive). Missing a land drop when holding 6 cards including a 4-mana Day of Judgment they want to cast next turn is a real cost - they need 4 lands untapped to cast Day of Judgment, and playing the Archive now would give them 6 lands next turn instead of 5.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed without playing Meticulous Archive from hand.
annotations.betterLine: Play Meticulous Archive to ensure hitting the 6th land and having maximum mana available going forward. This also enables surveil 1 for card quality.

annotations.description: Playing Meticulous Archive (enters tapped) instead of Sunbillow Verge as the land drop. With 4 lands already on board (Hallowed Fountain, Plains, Floodfarm Verge, Sunbillow Verge), Sunbillow Verge would enter and can tap for W (since Plains is controlled) or R. Playing Sunbillow Verge untapped would leave 5 mana available, enough to cast Day of Judgment (2WW) with mana open. Playing Meticulous Archive tapped means only 4 mana available. While the surveil 1 from Archive has some value, the tempo loss of an enters-tapped land is notable. Additionally, the player could have played Sunbillow Verge and then cast Consult the Star Charts or held up No More Lies with 5 lands untapped. The surveil 1 is a minor upside but the tempo difference matters, especially when holding Day of Judgment and counter magic.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Meticulous Archive (enters tapped) as land drop for turn 5.
annotations.betterLine: Play Sunbillow Verge untapped instead, keeping 5 mana available to hold up Day of Judgment or No More Lies + other interaction. The surveil 1 is minor compared to having full mana available.

annotations.description: Kimi25 has Sunbillow Verge in hand and hasn't played a land this turn. They should play the land first before casting Consult the Star Charts, since Consult looks at the top X cards where X is the number of lands they control. Playing the land first would mean looking at 6 cards instead of 5, giving better card selection. Additionally, having more mana available after resolving the spell could be relevant for holding up interaction.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Consult the Star Charts with 5 lands on the battlefield, looking at only 5 cards.
annotations.betterLine: Play Sunbillow Verge first (6 lands), then cast Consult the Star Charts to look at 6 cards instead of 5, improving card selection.

Additionally, Into the Flood Maw is in the graveyard, so Eddymurk Crab costs {4}{U}{U} - still expensive but approaching castable range. Countering the card selection spell would be a clean use of Spell Snare.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Spell Snare targeting Consult the Star Charts to deny the opponent card selection from their top 6 cards. Spell Snare is a narrow counterspell that may not find many other targets, and this is a good use for it.

annotations.description: Chose Hallowed Fountain from Consult the Star Charts when Jeskai Revelation was available. Jeskai Revelation is a powerful finisher that could be cast as early as next turn with 7 mana, and the hand was full of reactive spells but lacked a proactive win condition.

annotations.betterLine: Choose Jeskai Revelation - a game-winning spell that provides bounce, 4 damage, two prowess tokens, two cards, and 4 life, castable next turn with 7 mana available.

annotations.description: Rest in Peace could have been cast here to proactively exile graveyards and prevent future graveyard synergies. The opponent has Into the Flood Maw in their graveyard, and importantly, the opponent appears to be playing a blue deck that likely runs Eddymurk Crab (which costs less for each instant/sorcery in graveyard). Casting Rest in Peace now would be a proactive enchantment that provides ongoing value by exiling all future cards that would go to graveyards, making Eddymurk Crab much more expensive. Additionally, the opponent has 5 mana open including only blue sources, so countermagic is a concern - but passing with no development at all is also questionable when there's a proactive enchantment available.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed the turn without casting anything, holding all mana open with no instant-speed plays available.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Rest in Peace to proactively shut down graveyard synergies (particularly Eddymurk Crab cost reduction) and exile the existing graveyard cards. Even if countered, it would force the opponent to spend mana and a counter spell.

annotations.description: Used the more flexible counterspell (Spider-Sense) when the narrow one (Spell Snare) would have worked perfectly. Spell Snare costs only {U} vs Spider-Sense's {1}{U}, saving 1 mana this turn. More importantly, Spider-Sense is a broader answer that hits any instant, sorcery, or triggered ability, while Spell Snare only hits MV 2 spells. Using the narrow answer when applicable preserves the flexible one for future threats. The player's reasoning was also incorrect - they claimed Spider-Sense draws a card, which it does not.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Spider-Sense ({1}{U}) to counter Glacial Dragonhunt
annotations.betterLine: Cast Spell Snare ({U}) to counter Glacial Dragonhunt (MV 2), saving Spider-Sense for a future threat that Spell Snare couldn't answer, and saving 1 mana this turn

The player's reasoning ('Spider-Sense copies a spell!') is completely wrong about what the card does. By targeting their own Glacial Dragonhunt with Spider-Sense, they are countering their own spell, losing both cards for nothing. This wastes two cards and the mana spent casting both spells.
annotations.actionTaken: Cast Spider-Sense targeting their own Glacial Dragonhunt, countering their own spell due to misunderstanding Spider-Sense as a copy effect.
annotations.betterLine: Do not cast Spider-Sense here at all. Let Glacial Dragonhunt resolve to draw a card and potentially deal 3 damage. Save Spider-Sense to counter an opponent's spell on a future turn.

annotations.description: Eddymurk Crab is a 5/5 that costs {5}{U}{U} but gets {1} cheaper for each instant/sorcery in the graveyard. Sonnet Vorthos has 3 instants/sorceries in graveyard (Into the Flood Maw, Glacial Dragonhunt, Spider-Sense), so it costs {2}{U}{U} - very efficiently costed for a 5/5 that also taps up to two creatures on entry. This is a major threat that Kimi25 had multiple answers for. No More Lies would counter it unless opponent pays {3} (they have 5 lands but may not have 3 extra mana after casting the Crab for 4 mana - they'd have exactly 1 mana left, so they cannot pay {3}). Tishana's Tidebinder could counter the ETB trigger but still leaves a 5/5 on board. Get Lost could destroy it but gives two Map tokens. No More Lies was clearly the best option here - it would cleanly counter the Crab since the opponent tapped 4 of their 5 lands to cast it and cannot pay {3}. Instead, Kimi25 let a 5/5 resolve that will also tap two of their permanents.

annotations.betterLine: Cast No More Lies targeting Eddymurk Crab. The opponent has only 1 untapped land remaining after casting the 4-mana Crab, so they cannot pay the {3} tax, and the Crab would be exiled cleanly.

They could cast Get Lost now and still have mana for Tidebinder or No More Lies on the opponent's turn.

Tidebinder is a 3/2 that counters activated/triggered abilities, but the Crab's ETB has already resolved. Tidebinder doesn't remove the 5/5 Crab - it just puts a 3/2 body on board that can't profitably block it. Get Lost would actually destroy the Crab, which is the main threat. However, Tidebinder does add a body to the board and preserves Get Lost for later, and Kimi25 also has Day of Judgment as a backup plan. The Crab represents a significant clock (5 damage per turn), so removing it now with Get Lost might be more urgent. That said, playing Tidebinder develops the board and keeps removal options open, so this is debatable.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Get Lost targeting Eddymurk Crab to immediately remove the 5/5 threat, then deploy Tidebinder on a future turn when its counter ability might be relevant

Having three Spell Snares is redundant - they're narrow and situational, only useful against exactly 2-mana spells. Spider-Sense can also be cast for just U with its web-slinging cost if a creature is available, and it hits things Spell Snare cannot (like Day of Judgment, Jeskai Revelation, or triggered abilities).

annotations.description: Jeskai Revelation is a 7-mana spell on the stack that will deal 4 damage, bounce a permanent, create two tokens, draw two cards, and gain 4 life. This is a massive swing spell that should be the target of the bounce effect itself. By choosing to bounce an opponent's Steam Vents (an untapped land), Kimi25 is allowing Jeskai Revelation to fully resolve - the opponent gets all the benefits (4 damage, 2 tokens, 2 cards, 4 life gain) while only losing a land temporarily. Bouncing the Jeskai Revelation spell itself would counter it entirely (returning it to the opponent's hand without any of its effects resolving), which is enormously better. Alternatively, Kimi25 has countermagic in hand (No More Lies, Spell Snare) but those can't counter a 7-mana spell effectively. Wait - actually, Kimi25 is the one being targeted by Jeskai Revelation and is selecting the target for the bounce effect. Looking more carefully: the opponent cast Jeskai Revelation, and Kimi25 is being asked to select the target for the 'return target spell or permanent to its owner's hand' part. Actually, re-reading: it says 'Select a spell or permanent' and one of the choices IS Jeskai Revelation itself. If Kimi25 bounces Jeskai Revelation back to the opponent's hand, the spell would be returned to hand and the rest of its effects would still resolve (since the spell is already on the stack resolving). So bouncing the spell itself doesn't fizzle it. However, bouncing Steam Vents is still a very low-value choice. Kimi25 could bounce their own Seam Rip to replay it later, or bounce the opponent's land. But the real question is: why didn't Kimi25 counter Jeskai Revelation with No More Lies (costs WU, opponent has 4 untapped lands but needs to pay 3 extra)? The opponent has Steam Vents, Riverpyre Verge, Island, and potentially one more untapped - they have exactly 4 untapped mana sources, so they could pay the 3. Actually looking at the board: Sonnet Vorthos has Steam Vents (untapped), Riverpyre Verge (untapped), Island (untapped) = 3 untapped lands, so they could pay exactly 3. So No More Lies wouldn't work. But bouncing a random land instead of something more impactful is still suboptimal. The real issue is the target choice - bouncing an opponent's untapped Steam Vents is nearly meaningless when they have plenty of other lands. Kimi25 should bounce their own Seam Rip (to replay it as a reusable removal spell) or even Cori Mountain Monastery for value.
annotations.actionTaken: Chose to bounce opponent's Steam Vents (an untapped dual land) with Jeskai Revelation's bounce effect
annotations.betterLine: Bounce Kimi25's own Seam Rip to be able to replay it later as repeatable removal, or bounce a more impactful permanent. Bouncing a land when the opponent has 8 lands is nearly meaningless.

annotations.description: Kimi25 declined to counter Jeskai Revelation, a 7-mana spell that deals 4 damage, bounces a permanent, creates two tokens, draws two cards, and gains 4 life. This is an enormous swing card that represents a massive card advantage and tempo shift. Kimi25 had two copies of No More Lies in hand and 8 untapped lands available (the board shows several lands, enough to cast No More Lies for WU). The opponent at 13 life is casting this at 9 life Kimi25, meaning the 4 damage brings Kimi25 to 5 life while the opponent gains 4 life going to 17, creates two prowess tokens as threats, draws two cards, and bounces a Steam Vents. The life swing alone is 8 points, plus the card advantage and board presence. No More Lies would counter it unless the opponent pays 3, and the opponent has only 4 lands untapped (Steam Vents, Riverpyre Verge, Island, and one more) - wait, looking more carefully, the opponent has Steam Vents, Riverpyre Verge, Island untapped. That's 3 untapped lands, so the opponent could potentially pay the 3 mana for No More Lies. However, the opponent just cast a 7-mana spell, so they likely used most of their mana. Let me recount: opponent has 8 lands, Jeskai Revelation costs 7 (4URW), so they'd have 1 land untapped at most. They could NOT pay the additional 3 for No More Lies. This was a clear counter opportunity that would have exiled a devastating spell.
annotations.actionTaken: Passed priority and allowed Jeskai Revelation to resolve, taking 4 damage (going to 5 life), losing a Steam Vents to bounce, letting opponent create two Monk tokens, draw two cards, and gain 4 life.
annotations.betterLine: Cast No More Lies targeting Jeskai Revelation. The opponent spent 7 mana on it and would have at most 1 mana untapped, making it impossible to pay the additional 3. This would exile the Revelation and prevent an enormous swing in the opponent's favor.
